objectives: Use the sine rule to find a side or an angle.
Use the cosine rule for two sides and the included angle, or three sides.
Find the area of a triangle using ½ab sin C.

blocks.title: Sine rule
blocks.md: In triangle ABC with sides a, b, c opposite angles A, B, C. Use it when you know a side and its opposite angle plus one more angle or side:

blocks.title: Cosine rule and area
blocks.md: Use the cosine rule for two sides and the included angle (to find the third side), or for three sides (to find an angle). The area uses two sides and the included angle:
blocks.tex: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A \qquad \cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc} \qquad \text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C

blocks.title: Which rule?
blocks.md:
- Know **two angles and a side**, or two sides and a non-included angle: **sine rule**.
- Know **two sides and the included angle**, or **three sides**: **cosine rule**.
- Always label the triangle first (side a opposite angle A) and keep your calculator in degree mode.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Mixing up which angle is opposite which side.
- In the cosine rule, doing $(b^2 + c^2 - 2bc) \cos A$: multiply 2bc by cos A **before** subtracting.
- Rounding too early: keep at least 4 significant figures until the end.

blocks.title: Example 1: sine rule
blocks.statement: In triangle ABC, a = 8 cm, B = 40° and C = 65°. Find the angle A and the sides b and c (to 2 decimal places).

blocks.title: Example 2: cosine rule and area
blocks.statement: In a triangle, b = 7 cm, c = 9 cm and the included angle A = 60°. Find a and the area (2 d.p.). Then find the largest angle of a triangle with sides 5, 6 and 7 cm.
steps: Largest angle is opposite 7: cos C = (25 + 36 − 49) ÷ 60 = 0.2, so C ≈ 78.46°.

objectives: Find lengths in a cuboid and pyramid using Pythagoras in 3-D.
Find the angle between a line and a plane.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.md:
1. Draw the 3-D figure and pick out **right-angled triangles** (one at a time, as a plane picture).
2. Use Pythagoras to find lengths such as a diagonal of the base.
3. The **angle between a line and a plane** is the angle between the line and its **projection** on the plane (the shadow).
4. Then use sin, cos or tan in the right-angled triangle.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using a slanted length as a height; heights are perpendicular to the base.
- Measuring the angle from the wrong line: it must be from the line to its projection.
- Redrawing the triangle with the wrong sides: always write the sides you are using.

blocks.title: Example 1: cuboid
blocks.statement: A cuboid ABCDEFGH has AB = 8 cm, BC = 6 cm and CG = 5 cm. Find the diagonal AG and the angle it makes with the base.
steps: Angle GAC: tan θ = CG ÷ AC = 5 ÷ 10, so θ ≈ 26.6°.

blocks.title: Example 2: pyramid
blocks.statement: A pyramid has a square base of side 6 cm and its apex is 4 cm vertically above the centre of the base. Find the length of a sloping edge and the angle it makes with the base.
steps: Half the base diagonal = ½ × 6√2 = 3√2 ≈ 4.243 cm (its square is 18).
Angle with base: tan θ = 4 ÷ √18, so θ ≈ 43.3°.

exercises.prompt: In triangle PQR, p = 12, q = 9 and P = 80°. Find angle Q (1 d.p.).
exercises.explanation: sin Q = 9 sin 80° ÷ 12 = 0.7386, so Q = 47.6° (Q must be acute because q < p).
